Here is an incident report draft. Give me (1) a five-line summary, (2) the root cause in one sentence, (3) what is missing or unclear in the report.

INCIDENT REPORT 2026-041: Card payments declined at checkout

Summary
On Wednesday 21 October between 18:42 and 19:57 local time, roughly 31 percent of card payments on the web store were declined with a generic error. Payments through the mobile app were not affected. An estimated 1,140 orders were abandoned during the window. The issue was resolved by rolling back a configuration change to the payment gateway client.

Timeline
18:30 A routine configuration deploy raised the connection pool size for the gateway client from 20 to 80 on all six web nodes, in preparation for the sale weekend.
18:42 Decline rate begins to climb. No alert fires because the alert is based on HTTP 5xx responses, and declines are returned as HTTP 200 with an error body.
19:05 Customer support notices a spike in chats about failed payments and posts in the general engineering channel.
19:12 The on-call engineer is paged manually. She initially suspects the card provider, whose status page shows no problems.
19:31 A second engineer joins and notices gateway responses containing the text 'too many concurrent sessions for merchant'.
19:44 The pool size change is identified as the only recent change. Rollback is started.
19:57 Rollback complete on all nodes. Decline rate returns to the normal 2 to 3 percent.

Cause
The payment gateway enforces a limit of 250 concurrent sessions per merchant account. With six nodes at 80 connections each, the theoretical maximum became 480. Under evening load the real number crossed 250 and the gateway began rejecting new sessions. The limit is documented in the gateway's integration guide but was not known to the team making the change. The mobile app uses a separate merchant account and so was unaffected.

What went well
Rollback was fast once the cause was known. Support escalated quickly.

What went badly
Detection relied on customers complaining. The change was not tested under load. The on-call engineer did not have access to the gateway's merchant dashboard.

Follow-up actions
Add an alert on payment decline rate. Document gateway limits in the service README. Review who has dashboard access.
Write the customer-facing apology email for people whose payments failed. Keep it under 120 words and do not mention connection pools.

Below is a product spec from our PM. Turn it into a list of user stories with acceptance criteria.

Feature: Saved filters for the orders list

Background. Operations staff spend most of their day in the orders list. They apply the same combinations of filters over and over: for example 'unpaid, older than 7 days, wholesale customers' or 'shipped today from the Brisbane warehouse'. Today every filter has to be rebuilt by hand after each page reload, and people keep the combinations they need on sticky notes. In interviews, four of six operations staff named this as their biggest daily annoyance.

What we want. A user can save the current set of filters, the sort order and the visible columns under a name. Saved filters appear in a dropdown above the list. Choosing one applies it immediately. A user can rename, update and delete their own saved filters. One saved filter can be marked as the default and is applied automatically when the user opens the orders list.

Sharing. A user with the team lead role can mark a saved filter as shared with their team. Shared filters appear for everyone in the team in a separate section of the dropdown and cannot be edited by ordinary members, but a member can make a personal copy. If a team lead deletes a shared filter that someone uses as their default, that person falls back to the standard unfiltered view and sees a one-time notice explaining why.

Limits. Each user can have up to 25 personal saved filters. Names are unique per user, at most 40 characters. Relative dates such as 'today' or 'last 7 days' must be stored as relative, not as the fixed dates they resolved to at the time of saving.

Out of scope for the first release: sharing between teams, scheduling exports from a saved filter, and saved filters on any list other than orders.

Success measure. Within a month of release at least half of active operations users have created one saved filter, and median time from opening the list to first row click drops by 20 percent.
